value.overview: The White-eared Ground-Sparrow is a secretive, ground-dwelling New World sparrow of Middle America. It usually lives in dense understory, tangled second growth, forest edges, ravines, and well-vegetated gardens at middle elevations. Although it spends much of its time on or near the ground, it often sings from low perches. In Costa Rica, it is a resident species found mainly in suitable habitats on the Pacific slope and in parts of the Central Valley.
value.classification: The White-eared Ground-Sparrow belongs to the family Passerellidae, the New World sparrows, and the genus Melozone. Its scientific name is Melozone leucotis.
value.identification: This is a fairly large, robust sparrow, about 17–18 cm long, with a short dark bill and a long, rounded tail. Adults have generally olive-brown upperparts, pale underparts, a rufous or chestnut crown, and a distinctive white patch around the ear and cheek. Dark markings through the eye and along the sides of the face provide contrast. It is often detected by movement in dense vegetation, where its subdued colors and low, skulking habits make it easy to overlook.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from southern Mexico through Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it reaches the northern limit of its range and occurs locally, especially on the Pacific slope, in foothills, the Central Valley, and areas such as Monteverde where suitable cover remains. It favors dense thickets, forest edges, ravines, humid or semi-open woodland, unmanaged secondary growth, coffee landscapes, and large gardens. Most records are from middle elevations, commonly around 500–1,500 meters.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and generally non-migratory. Individuals defend territories throughout the year, although local movements or temporary changes in detectability may occur.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place in dense ground-level or low vegetation. The female builds a bulky cup or bowl from stems, twigs, and other plant material, usually on the ground or less than about 75 cm above it, concealed among thick plants such as bananas, orchids, grasses, or shrubs. A typical clutch contains two white eggs marked with brown. The female performs most incubation, which lasts roughly 12–14 days, while the male helps feed the nestlings.
value.dietFeeding: The White-eared Ground-Sparrow forages mainly on the ground and in low vegetation. Its diet includes seeds, small fruits, and invertebrates such as insects and other arthropods. It commonly searches beneath dense cover, scratching or moving through leaf litter and tangled plants. During the breeding season, animal food is particularly important for adults feeding growing young. Its short, sturdy bill is well suited to handling seeds and probing among vegetation.
value.behavior: This species is generally shy, terrestrial, and difficult to observe in open situations. It moves quietly through thickets, often in pairs or as a territorial adult, and may freeze or retreat when approached. Males sing from low perches to advertise territories and attract mates. White-eared Ground-Sparrows can persist in some suburban and urban forest remnants in Costa Rica, but they depend on dense vegetation and avoid highly open, intensively developed areas.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly documented, but the species is not currently considered globally threatened.
